rows.synopsis: When Cody wants to visit her favorite tree but the park is closed, she makes a new plan.
rows.situation: Cody has one plan all morning: a trip to the park to sit under her favorite cherry blossom tree, and the park is closed when she gets there. Instead of sulking about the lost trip, she interviews herself and finds a new goal, build the tree at home.
rows.coping: Cody names the letdown and immediately reframes it: if she cannot go to the tree, she will make the tree. She breaks the new goal into three small jobs, paper, cutting, gluing, and checks each one off with a ding, and imagination finishes the job her feet could not.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis stops at makes a new plan; the script shows the self-talk trick, the three-job plan with check-off dings, and the closing imagination game (Antarctica). confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Cody plans a visit to her favorite cherry blossom tree, and the park is closed. So she asks herself the Helpster question, is there another way, and lands on building the tree herself. Three small jobs later, paper cut and glued into a very lifelike tree, she is sniffing imaginary blossoms and using the same imagination to visit Antarctica and play with penguins.

rows.synopsis: There are many ways to be a Helpster, as Cody demonstrates, from dancing and singing to, most importantly, helping people.
rows.situation: Cody walks viewers through becoming an honorary Helpster, and the training is mostly play: smiling, moving fast, dancing, singing. The real test comes mid-video when Mr. Primm calls asking for help, and Cody models the most Helpster move of all, asking how you can help.
rows.coping: Cody turns a checklist of monster skills into an invitation to copy along, and when a real request for help arrives she finishes her commitment first (a proper goodbye), then answers the call, showing that helping fits inside ordinary routines.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis lists the demonstrations; the script shows the step-by-step honorary training, the mid-episode phone call from Mr. Primm, and the ask-how-you-can-help lesson stated as Cody's favorite thing ever. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Cody teaches everyone watching how to be a Helpster, which starts with being a monster: smile like a monster, zoom like a monster, dance like a monster, sing like a monster. Job two is finding a way to help, and Cody runs a list from toy cleanup to playing quietly so someone can rest. Then Mr. Primm calls needing help, and Cody wraps up her video politely and answers, because the best Helpster move is simply asking how you can help.

rows.synopsis: Joined by her friend Amazing Alie, Cody shows us how to play games with our friends who are far away.
rows.situation: Cody wants to play a game with a faraway friend, so she and Amazing Alie turn a video call into a scavenger hunt where each round demands a directional word: something green next to the chair, something wooden under a toy elephant.
rows.coping: The episode solves missing-a-friend with play, a shared game with rules both players can follow from their own rooms, and Cody's exaggerations about her toy menagerie keep the distance feeling small and funny.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis names the game and guest; the script shows how directional words (next to, under, between) structure each round, Alie's green plant find, Cody's wooden spoon under elephant Lulu, and the rocket-ship toy gag. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Cody rings up her friend Amazing Alie for a long-distance scavenger hunt: one player names a thing, the other hunts it down and describes where they found it. Alie fetches a green plant from next to her chair; Cody digs a wooden spoon out from under her elephant Lulu, who is busy balancing on top of Julian the rhinoceros inside a rocket ship bound for space. Everyone watching learns they can run the same game with faraway friends and family.

rows.synopsis: Cody loves giving people high-fives and handshakes, but what should she do when people are not close enough to reach?
rows.situation: Cody loves high fives and handshakes and runs into the limits of them: someone might be too far away, on a screen instead of in the room, or might simply say no thank you to the contact. She invents two greetings that work for everyone.
rows.coping: When a beloved routine does not fit the moment, Cody does not force it. She invents substitutes, bright smiles and hand waves, that work across distance, over video, and even into a mirror, and respects a no thank you as a reason to adapt, not a problem.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis poses the distance question; the script adds the consent wrinkle (someone saying no thank you to a high five) and the song delivery of the answer. confidence high. catalog synopsis restructured to remove dashes.
rows.per_story_synopsis: High fives and handshakes are Cody's love language, and she keeps meeting moments where they cannot happen: a friend too far away to reach, a video call, or someone who would rather not be touched. Her fix is a pair of greetings with no reach required, delivered as a song: bright smiles and hand waves, warm as sunlight from a distance. Anyone can use them on faraway friends, on video, or on their own reflection.

rows.synopsis: The Helpsters are used to being together in person. Now that they're apart, they make a new plan so they can still have fun with friends.
rows.situation: Cody loves being in the room with Mr. Primm, Heart, and Scatter, and the friends are apart. Instead of just missing them, she invents ways the distance can be crossed: cards, drawings, phone calls, video chats, and a four-way song written together over the phone.
rows.coping: Cody names the ache of missing friends and answers it with a plan, staying in touch on purpose: sending made things, calling, reading books together, and making music as a group even through a phone line.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis keeps it general; the script shows the specific bridge, the four-way phone call where the friends compose and sing It sure feels like we're together together, plus Heart's painting of Cody in the same outfit. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: Cody's favorite thing is being with Mr. Primm, Heart, and Scatter, and today the friends are far apart. So they find the together-anyway moves: Heart mails a painting of Cody in matching clothes, friends trade cards and handmade gifts, and the whole crew gathers on one phone call to write and sing a song about reaching out. Being apart, it turns out, is a plan problem, and the Helpsters have a plan.

rows.synopsis: Cody is joined by special musical guests Grouplove for a song to thank everyone who's keeping us safe, happy, and healthy.
rows.situation: Cody wants to thank all the people whose work keeps everyone safe and cared for, far too many helpers to thank one by one. She and the band Grouplove build a thank-you song out of looped everyday sounds when no instruments are on hand.
rows.coping: Gratitude gets made into something: a song built by looping claps and sounds, a long spoken list of helpers from health care workers to janitors, and a special thank you to kids who lend grown-ups a hand.
rows.notes: script_vs_synopsis: the synopsis names the song and guests; the script shows the loop-your-sounds invention when the band arrives without instruments, the catalog of helpers named by job, and the direct praise for kids helping at home. confidence high.
rows.per_story_synopsis: So many people are holding everything up right now, and Cody wants to thank every one of them. When Grouplove shows up with no instruments, they loop everyday sounds instead, do something again and again until it becomes music, and sing a thank you to the workers who run packages, medicine, electricity, and care. Cody adds her own spoken list, from firefighters to grocery clerks to teachers, and saves a special proud moment for the kids who are helping the grown-ups.
